question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
title: Single Responsibility Principle Explained
direct_answer: **SRP** states that a class should have only **one reason to change** — meaning it should encapsulate exactly one responsibility. If a class handles user logic, email sending, AND database persistence, any of those three concerns can force a change, making the class fragile and hard to maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why separation of concerns matters at the class level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining SRP vaguely as 'do one thing' without explaining 'one reason to change'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete before/after example showing how splitting a class reduces coupling

sections.title: What SRP Really Means
sections.content: SRP is the first SOLID principle by Robert C. Martin. The key phrase is **'one reason to change'** — not 'one method'. A class should own one cohesive concern, so only changes to that concern force a rewrite.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A class should have **one reason to change**
- Violations: a class that validates, persists to DB, AND sends email
- Fix: split into `UserValidator`, `UserRepository`, `EmailService`
- Benefits: easier to test, less coupling, easier to understand
- SRP applies to methods and modules too

sections.title: Violation vs Fix
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: SRP means a class should have only one reason to change. If a class is doing validation, database persistence, and email sending, changes to email logic could break persistence code. The fix is to split them into UserValidator, UserRepository, and EmailService. Each now has a single owner and a single reason to be modified.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot service applying SOLID principles to an order processing module
speakable_v2.hook: One class, one job — the moment a class has two reasons to change, you've already got a maintenance headache waiting to happen.

beats.text: SRP says every class should have exactly one reason to change. That's Robert Martin's phrasing — and it's more precise than 'do one thing'. A class owns a single concern, so only changes to that concern should force you to edit it.

Without SRP, one class becomes a change magnet. Touch the email logic, you risk breaking the database logic — even though they're unrelated. Splitting by responsibility isolates blast radius and makes each class easier to reason about.

items: UserValidator — owns validation rules; changes when validation logic changes
UserRepository — owns DB persistence; changes when schema or ORM changes
EmailService — owns notification; changes when email templates or providers change

beats.text: In a Spring Boot order processing module, OrderService.placeOrder() might call a validator, a repository, and a notification sender — but each lives in its own class. The OrderService orchestrates; it doesn't implement all three. candidates miss: if you see a class that imports javax.mail AND javax.persistence AND has validation logic, that's a three-concern class — classic SRP violation.

items: Don't confuse 'one method' with SRP — a UserRepository with save, find, update, and delete is still single-responsibility.
Watch for names with 'And' or 'Manager' covering unrelated things — those usually signal multiple concerns crammed together.

speakable_v2.cap: If you can give more than one independent answer to 'why would this class change?' — it's an SRP violation.

question: How do you identify an SRP violation in existing code?
title: Identifying SRP Violations in Java Code
direct_answer: **SRP violations** are visible when a class has multiple unrelated reasons to change — large file size, names containing 'And', or imports from unrelated packages (e.g., javax.mail AND java.sql). The real test: ask 'why would this class change?' — more than one independent answer means SRP violation.

sections.title: Signs of SRP Violation
sections.content: Ask: **'Why would this class change?'** If you can list more than one independent reason, the class violates SRP. Large God Classes with 500+ lines are almost always violators.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Class name with 'And' or 'Manager' handling unrelated concerns
- Method groups serving completely different stakeholders
- High number of imports from unrelated packages
- Frequent merge conflicts by different teams on same class
- Hard to unit test because too many dependencies need mocking

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I look for red flags: a class whose name contains 'And', methods that fall into different concern buckets — some dealing with email, others with database saves — and imports from unrelated packages. The real test is asking 'why would this class change?' If I get more than one independent answer, it's an SRP violation.

speakable_v2.hook: The quickest SRP smell check? Ask one question — and if you get two independent answers, you've found your violation.

beats.text: An SRP violation is when a class has more than one independent reason to change. Identifying it means finding those separate concerns hiding inside a single file.
Violations creep in gradually — a feature here, a convenience method there. Over time classes become grab-bags. Catching them early keeps refactoring cheap.

items: Name smell: class named 'UserAndEmailService' or 'OrderManagerHelper' mixing unrelated concerns
Import smell: class imports javax.mail AND javax.persistence AND apache.commons.validator
Test smell: unit test needs five mocks just to test one method — each mock signals a dependency from a different concern

beats.text: In a Spring Boot order module, if OrderService has sendConfirmationEmail(), saveToDatabase(), and validateDiscount() — ask why it'd change. Email template change? Yes. Schema change? Yes. Discount rule change? Yes. Three independent reasons. production trap: when multiple teams edit the same class for different features, merge conflicts are a reliable sign of SRP violation in the wild.

items: Large class size is a hint, not a guarantee — a large repository with many CRUD methods can still follow SRP.
Don't reflexively split every class — only split when the concerns are truly independent and change for different reasons.

speakable_v2.cap: The 'why would this change?' question is your fastest SRP violation detector — use it in every code review.

question: How does SRP improve testability of Java classes?
title: SRP and Unit Testability in Java
direct_answer: **SRP improves testability** because a class with one responsibility has fewer dependencies to mock and a narrower test surface. When a class does three things, a unit test must set up mocks for all three concerns even when testing only one — SRP eliminates that overhead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connection between design principles and practical testing outcomes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying SRP is only about code organization without linking it to testing benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example comparing setup for a 3-dep class vs three 1-dep classes

sections.title: Why SRP Makes Testing Easier
sections.content: Unit tests are supposed to test **one thing in isolation**. When a class violates SRP, you need to inject and mock multiple unrelated dependencies just to test a single code path. SRP-compliant classes have minimal dependencies.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Fewer constructor dependencies → fewer mocks in @BeforeEach
- Test failures are immediately localized to the single responsibility
- SRP classes are easier to test in isolation (true unit tests)
- Changes to one class don't break unrelated test suites

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When a class follows SRP, it has very few constructor dependencies — maybe one or two. When I write a unit test, I only need one or two mocks, and the test is fast and focused. If a class violates SRP and handles validation, persistence, and email, I need to mock three different things just to test one code path. SRP keeps tests small, isolated, and easy to maintain.

seo.metaTitle: SRP and Testability | Java Design Principles Interview
seo.metaDescription: How Single Responsibility Principle improves unit testability in Java. Fewer mocks, focused tests, and better isolation.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot service applying SOLID principles to an order processing module
speakable_v2.hook: The number of mocks your test needs is a direct readout of how many responsibilities are crammed into the class under test.

beats.text: SRP improves testability because a class with one responsibility has at most one or two collaborators to mock. Fewer mocks means faster setup, faster tests, and failures that point directly at the broken responsibility.

Unit tests should isolate one unit of behavior. When a class violates SRP, every test drags in all concerns — you end up setting up three mocks to test one line of validation logic, which defeats the point.

items: SRP-compliant UserValidator: one dependency (maybe none), one mock — test is three lines
SRP-violating UserService: three dependencies (validator, repo, emailer) — even a simple test needs @BeforeEach with three when() stubs

beats.text: In a Spring Boot order module, OrderValidator has one constructor dependency: a discount rules loader. Its Mockito test mocks one thing and verifies one behavior. Compare that to an OrderService that also handles persistence and email — its test needs mocks for repository, email sender, and validator. non-obvious: when a test class grows to 200 lines, it's often because the production class violates SRP, not because the tests are complex.

items: Don't measure testability purely by test line count — a simple class can still have a verbose test if the domain is complex.
SRP alone doesn't make tests fast — you still need DI to inject mocks, which is why Spring constructor injection pairs so naturally with SRP.

speakable_v2.cap: Count your mocks — if you need more than two to test a class, it's probably doing more than one thing.

question: What is the difference between SRP and separation of concerns?
title: SRP vs Separation of Concerns in Java
direct_answer: **Separation of Concerns (SoC)** is the broad architectural principle that different concerns should be handled by different parts of the system — it applies at every level. **SRP** is SoC applied specifically at the **class level**, stating each class should encapsulate exactly one concern. SRP is a concrete application of SoC.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding — can you distinguish related principles?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating SRP and SoC as identical or using them interchangeably
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples at different levels: layered architecture (SoC) vs class-level (SRP)

rows: Controller vs Service vs Repository layers

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Separation of Concerns is the broad principle — different concerns like UI, business logic, and data access should be separated. We see it in MVC architecture. SRP is that same idea applied at the class level specifically. Every SRP-compliant system also has good separation of concerns, but SoC is the bigger umbrella.

question: Can a class have multiple methods and still follow SRP?
title: Multiple Methods and SRP Compliance in Java
direct_answer: **Yes** — a class can have many methods and still follow SRP as long as all those methods serve the **same single responsibility**. A `UserRepository` with `save()`, `findById()`, `delete()`, and `update()` has four methods but one responsibility: data access for User. Method count is irrelevant; concern count is what matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you truly understand SRP vs naive 'one method per class' misinterpretation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SRP means a class should have only one method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish clearly between method count and responsibility count

sections.title: Methods vs Responsibilities
sections.content: SRP is about **cohesion of purpose**, not about limiting method count. A `String` class has dozens of methods — they all serve one responsibility: string manipulation. As long as all methods relate to the same single concern, SRP is satisfied.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- SRP = one concern/responsibility, NOT one method
- `UserRepository` with CRUD methods follows SRP (all serve data access)
- Violation: adding `sendEmail()` to `UserRepository` — different concern
- Ask: 'Do all these methods change together for the same reason?'

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Absolutely — a class can have many methods and still follow SRP. What matters is whether all those methods serve the same single concern. A UserRepository with save, find, update, and delete has four methods but one responsibility: data access. The moment you add sendWelcomeEmail() to that repository, you've introduced a second responsibility and violated SRP.

seo.metaDescription: A class can have multiple methods and follow SRP. Learn the difference between method count and concern count in Java.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot service applying SOLID principles to an order processing module
speakable_v2.hook: SRP is about how many concerns a class has — not how many methods. Those are completely different things.

beats.text: SRP is about responsibility count, not method count. A class satisfies SRP as long as all its methods serve the same single concern — even if there are ten of them. The measure is cohesion of purpose, not lines of code.
The 'one method per class' misconception makes codebases absurdly fragmented. The real goal is that a class changes for one reason — and a class can have many methods all tied to that one reason.

items: UserRepository — has save(), findById(), update(), delete(). Four methods, one concern: data access for User entity.
Java String — has length(), substring(), toUpperCase(), contains(), and dozens more. One concern: string manipulation.
SRP violation — UserRepository also has sendWelcomeEmail(). Now it has two concerns: data access and notification.

beats.text: In a Spring Boot order module, OrderRepository might have findByStatus(), findByCustomerId(), save(), and deleteById() — all serve the same concern: persistence for Order. That's fine. The test is simple: do all these methods change together for the same reason? If yes, SRP holds. sharp edge: if two groups of methods in a class would change for different reasons — say, one group for DB schema changes and another for business rule changes — that's two responsibilities, regardless of how few methods there are.

items: Don't split every method into its own class — that creates fragmentation with no cohesion at all.
The question isn't 'how many methods?' but 'would all these methods change for the same reason?'

speakable_v2.cap: Ask whether all methods in the class change for the same reason — if yes, it's single-responsibility no matter the method count.
